HMRC must receive your tax return and any money you owe by the deadline.

If you do not know your profit for the whole tax year, you still need to send a tax return. Check how to send a return if you do not know your profit for the whole year.

The last tax year started on 6 April 2025 and ended on 5 April 2026. The deadline for earlier tax returns has passed and you may have to pay a penalty. Send your tax return or payment as soon as possible to avoid further penalties.

## Telling HMRC you need to complete a return

You must tell HMRC by 5 October if you need to complete a tax return for the previous year and you have either:

- never sent a tax return before

- registered before, but did not need to send a tax return for the tax year 2024 to 2025

You can tell HMRC by registering for Self Assessment. Check how to register for Self Assessment.

### If you register after 5 October 2026

HMRC will send you a letter or email. It will give you a different deadline to send your tax return by. The deadline will be 3 months from the date on the letter or email.

You must still pay the tax you owe by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027 or you'll get a penalty.

## Sending a paper tax return

You must send your paper tax return by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026. HMRC must receive it by then or you'll get a late filing penalty.

You can send it at any time on or after 6 April 2026. But it must reach HMRC by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026.

## Submitting an online tax return

You must submit your online tax return by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you'll get a late filing penalty.

If you want to pay your Self Assessment bill through your tax code, you must submit it by 11:59pm on 30 December 2026. If you miss this deadline, you'll have to pay another way.

You can submit your return any time on or after 6 April 2026 up to the deadline.

## Paying the tax you owe

You must pay your Self Assessment tax by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not pay by then, you'll get a penalty.

There is a second payment deadline of 31 July. This applies if you make 'payments on account' towards your bill.

You can estimate your Self Assessment tax bill before you send your tax return. You may want to do this to:

- find out what your bill is likely to be

- plan your money and pay on time

You can find help on understanding the tax you owe.

## Trustees of a registered pension scheme or non-resident companies

You must send a paper tax return. HMRC must get it by 31 January 2027.

You cannot send this return online.

You can send it any time on or after 6 April 2026. It must reach HMRC by 31 January 2027.

### Partnership returns if you have a company as a partner

If one of your partners is a limited company, and your partnership's accounting date is between 1 February and 5 April, your return must be filed by:

- 12 months from the accounting date if you file online
- 9 months from the accounting date if you file on paper

### Getting a penalty

You get a penalty if you need to complete a tax return and you:

- send your return late

- pay your tax bill late

### Work out your penalty

You can estimate your penalty for late Self Assessment tax returns and payments.

### If you register for Self Assessment late

If you register after 5 October and do not pay all of your tax bill by 31 January, you may get a 'failure to notify' penalty.

This penalty is based on the amount still left to pay. You will get it within 12 months after HMRC receives your Self Assessment tax return.

You can find more information on 'failure to notify' penalties.

## If you send your tax return late

You'll get these penalties for filing late:

- an initial £100 penalty

- after 3 months, additional daily penalties of £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900

- after 6 months, a further penalty of 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater

- after 12 months, another 5% or £300 charge, whichever is greater

To avoid this, send your Self Assessment tax return as soon as you can.

All partners will be charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.

## If you pay your tax late

You will get a penalty of 5% of the tax you have not paid. This happens at these times:

- 30 days
- 6 months
- 12 months

You will also be charged interest on the amount you owe. Pay your Self Assessment tax bill as soon as you can to avoid this.

Find out what happens if you do not pay your tax bill.

Your State Pension amount depends on your National Insurance record.

Check your State Pension forecast to find out how much you could get when you reach State Pension age. It shows your National Insurance record too.

The full rate of new State Pension is £241.30 a week. Your amount could be different depending on:

- if you were contracted out before 2016

- the number of National Insurance qualifying years you have

- if you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016

Find out what tax you might pay on your retirement income, including if you retire abroad.

## If you're getting less than £241.30 a week

You might need more National Insurance qualifying years to get a bigger State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started before April 2016

You may have been "contracted out." This means you or your employer paid more into your workplace or private pension, and less into your State Pension.

If you were contracted out, you will usually need more than 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of new State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started after April 2016

Your full new State Pension will need 35 qualifying years.

## If you're getting more than £241.30 a week

Before 2016, you may have paid into the Additional State Pension. At the same time, you may have would have got more State Pension if the old rules were still in place. If both of these are true, you'll get a 'protected payment'. This payment comes on top of the full rate of new State Pension.

### Annual increases

The new State Pension goes up each year by the highest of these three:

- how much average wages grew in Great Britain

- how much UK prices grew (measured by the Consumer Prices Index / CPI)

- 2.5%

If you have a protected payment, it goes up each year by the same amount as the CPI.

### There are 2 Child Benefit rates.

| Who the allowance is for | Rate (weekly) |
| --- | --- |
| Eldest or only child | £27.05 |
| Additional children | £17.90 per child |

### If you are paid too much or too little

You must contact the Child Benefit Office if you are paid too much or too little.

### The benefit cap

Child Benefit you get will count towards the benefit cap. If the cap affects you, you will still get the full amount of your Child Benefit. But your other benefits may be reduced.

## If families split up

If a family splits up, the eldest child gets £27.05 a week.

If you have 2 children and one lives with you and the other lives with someone else (for example, your ex-partner), you'll each get £27.05 a week.

If you both claim for the same child, only one of you will get Child Benefit for them.

If you're entitled to Child Benefit for any other children, you'll get £17.90 for each child.

## If families join together

If you move in with a partner who also claims Child Benefit, you get £27.05 for the eldest child in the household and £17.90 for any younger children.

You and your partner can claim for different children. If you live together, you cannot both claim at the higher rate. If you do, you may have to pay back some of the money.

You must report this change to your family circumstances.

## If you or your partner earn over the threshold

If either you or your partner's 'adjusted net income' is over the threshold, you may have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge.

Your adjusted net income is your total income before any personal allowances and less things like Gift Aid. Your total income includes interest from savings and dividends.

If you have to pay the charge, you can still get the other benefits of Child Benefit, like National Insurance credits. The charge will not be more than the amount you get in Child Benefit payments.

Use the Child Benefit tax calculator to work out if your adjusted net income is over the threshold. If it is, the calculator will also tell you how much charge you'll have to pay.

If both you and your partner have an individual income that's over the threshold, then whoever has the higher adjusted net income is responsible for paying the charge.

If either you or your partner has an individual income of £20,000 or more above the threshold (£10,000 or more before April 2024), you'll be charged the same amount as the Child Benefit payments you receive. You'll end up with no extra money from Child Benefit.

You can make a claim and opt out of getting payments if you do not want to pay the charge. You can still get the other benefits of Child Benefit, like National Insurance credits.

## If you're under 16

You can either claim for your own child, or the person responsible for you can claim for them instead. You'll usually get more if you claim yourself.

Universal Credit is paid monthly. Your payment amount depends on:

- your standard allowance
- any extra amounts that apply to you
- any money taken off your payment
- if you're working, how much you earn

Use a benefits calculator to see how much you could get.

If you get Universal Credit, you'll earn Class 3 National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension.

### Standard allowance

You get one standard allowance for your household.

| How much you get | Monthly standard allowance |

| If you are single and under 25 | £338.58 |

| If you are single and 25 or over | £424.90 |

| If you live with your partner and you are both under 25 | £528.34 (for both of you) |

| If you live with your partner and either of you are 25 or over | £666.97 (for both of you) |

## Extra amounts

You may get more money on top of your standard allowance if you're eligible.

You will need to report changes when you become eligible for an extra amount. They are not added automatically. For example, if you become a carer you need to tell DWP. The carer's element of Universal Credit is not automatically applied if you start getting Carer's Allowance.

### If you have children

You'll get £303.94 a month for each child that lives with you.

If your first child was born before 6 April 2017, you'll get an extra £47.94 a month for that child.

You get money for each child until the 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they're in eligible education or training – for example, they're studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

### If your child has a disability

You might get extra money each month if any of your children are disabled.

You'll either get:

- £164.79 - the lower amount

- £514.71 - the higher amount

The higher amount is for a child who:

- gets the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children

- gets the higher rate of the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

- is blind or severely sight impaired

The lower amount is for a child who gets any other rate of either DLA for children, or PIP.

### Childcare costs

You can claim back up to 85% of your childcare costs if you're working. If you live with your partner both of you need to be working, unless one of you is unable to work due to a disability or health condition.

The childcare needs to be from a registered provider. You can get help paying for childcare including nurseries, childminders, breakfast clubs, after school care and holiday clubs.

The most you can get each month is:

- £1,071.09 for one child

- £1,836.16 for 2 or more children

You need to pay your childcare costs up front and claim the money back as part of your payment. You can get support to help you pay your childcare costs up front. Talk to your work coach after you've made your claim.

Read more about childcare costs and Universal Credit.

### If you have a disability or health condition

You might get extra money each month if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

| How much you'll get | Extra monthly amount |

| If you have a severe health condition or disability that's unlikely to change or you are nearing the end of your life | £429.80 |

| If your health condition or disability is assessed as less severe or your condition may improve over time | £217.26 |

There are different rules if you reported a health condition before 6 April 2026.

If you live with your partner and you both have limited capability for work and work-related activity, you'll only get one extra monthly amount. You'll get the higher amount if one of you is eligible for it.

If you get the severe disability premium and you're moving to Universal Credit, you might also be entitled to a 'transitional protection' payment.

Read more about health conditions, disability and Universal Credit.

### If you care for someone who gets a health or disability-related benefit

You could get an extra amount known as a 'carer's element'. This is added to your Universal Credit if you care for someone who gets one of the following benefits:

- Adult Disability Payment – standard or enhanced award

- Armed Forces Independence Payment

- Attendance Allowance

- Child Disability Payment – middle or highest care award

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate, intermediate rate or exceptional rate with Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Disability Living Allowance – middle or highest care rate

- Personal Independence Payment – either rate of the daily living part

You need to provide care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

You'll get an extra monthly amount of £209.34. If you live with your partner and you both care for the same person, you'll only get one extra monthly amount.

You may also be eligible for Carer's Allowance.

This is on top of any extra amount you get if you have a disabled child.

If you are getting an extra amount because you have limited capability for work and work related activity (LCWRA), you cannot also get the carer's element.

If the person you care for gets the severe disability premium, it will stop when you claim the carer's element of Universal Credit.

### Housing costs

You could get money to help pay your housing costs. The payment can cover rent and some service charges.

If you're a homeowner, you might be able to get a loan to help with interest payments on your mortgage.

## Money taken off your payment

Your payment might be reduced if any of the following apply:

- you are paying back an advance on a Universal Credit payment

- you would get above the amount limited by the benefit cap

- you've been overpaid benefits in the past

- you owe money for Council Tax, court fines, electricity, gas, water or Child Maintenance

- you pay your gas or electricity bill directly from your Universal Credit payment

- you have a paid job

- you have other income – for example, money from pensions or certain other benefits

- you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments

If you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments, your payment will be reduced by £4.35 for every £250 you have between £6,000 and £16,000. Another £4.35 is taken off for any leftover amount that is not a full £250.

Find out more about money taken off your Universal Credit payment.

### Benefits that affect how much Universal Credit you get

You can get Universal Credit at the same time as other benefits. Your Universal Credit payment will be reduced by the same amount as the other benefit's payment. This applies when you get Universal Credit and any of the following benefits:

- Armed Forces Pensions

- Carer's Allowance

- Carer Support Payment (Scotland)

- Incapacity Benefit

- Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (but not any increases for needing constant attendance or for the most severe disablement)

- Maternity Allowance

- Severe Disablement Allowance

- State Pension

- Widowed Mother's Allowance

- Widowed Parent's Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

- New Style Jobseeker's Allowance (JSA)

### Claiming Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA

You might be able to get Universal Credit at the same time as New Style ESA or JSA. If you do, your Universal Credit payment is reduced by the amount you get for New Style ESA or JSA.

New Style ESA and JSA are paid more often than Universal Credit.

You'll also get different National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension and can help you qualify for other benefits.

If your circumstances change and your Universal Credit payment is reduced or stops, you might continue to get New Style ESA or JSA. This could happen if:

- your partner's income increases

- you have more than £16,000 in savings

Check if you're eligible for:

- New Style Jobseeker's Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance

## Moving to Universal Credit from other benefits

If you have applied for Universal Credit, you will keep getting your current benefit paid for 2 more weeks. You must still be eligible for your current benefit.

This only applies if you are getting income-related Employment and Support Allowance or Housing Benefit.

You will not need to pay back the extra payments. The extra payments will not affect the Universal Credit you might get.

If you have received a Migration Notice letter telling you to claim Universal Credit, you might also get a 'transitional protection' payment.

## If your Universal Credit claim is reviewed

Your claim might be reviewed. This is to check that you are getting the right payment and the right support. Find out more about [Universal Credit reviews](#).
You may be able to get Carer's Allowance if you, the person you care for and the type of care you provide meet certain rules.

## The person you care for

The person you care for must already get one of these benefits:

- Personal Independence Payment - daily living component
- Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Attendance Allowance
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- Constant Attendance Allowance at or above the normal maximum rate with an Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit
- Constant Attendance Allowance at the basic (full day) rate with a War Disablement Pension
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- Child Disability Payment - the middle or highest care rate
- Adult Disability Payment - daily living component at the standard or enhanced rate

### If you care for the person with others

You cannot get Carer's Allowance if you share the care of someone and the other carer is already claiming any of these for that person:

- Carer's Allowance
- Carer Support Payment
- the extra amount of Universal Credit for caring for someone who gets a disability-related benefit

If you want to get Carer's Allowance, talk to the other carer about changing their benefits.

If the other carer does not want to change their benefits, you can still apply for Carer's Allowance. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) will decide who should get the benefit.

## The type of care you provide

You must spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone. This can include:

- helping them wash and cook
- taking them to a doctor's appointment
- helping around the home, like managing bills and shopping

## Your eligibility

All of the following must be true:

- you're 16 or over

- you spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone

- you've been in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years (this does not apply if you're a refugee or have humanitarian protection status)

- you normally live in England or Wales, or you live abroad as a member of the armed forces (you might still be eligible if you're moving to or already living in an EEA country or Switzerland)

- you're not in full-time education

- you're not studying for 21 hours a week or more

- immigration rules do not control how long you can stay in the UK

- your earnings are £204 or less a week after tax, National Insurance and expenses

If you live in Scotland, you need to apply for Carer Support Payment instead of Carer's Allowance.

If you're from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein, you and your family usually also need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme to get Carer's Allowance. The deadline to apply was 30 June 2021 for most people, but you might still be able to apply. Check if you can still apply to the EU Settlement Scheme.

### Calculating your earnings

Your earnings are any income you get from a job or self-employment. You work this out after taking off tax, National Insurance and expenses.

Expenses can include:

- 50% of your pension contributions

- equipment you need to do your job, for example specialist clothing

- travel between different workplaces that your employer does not pay for, for example fuel or train fares

- business costs if you're self-employed, for example a computer you only use for work

If you pay a carer to look after the disabled person or your children while you work, you can treat care costs that are less than or equal to 50% of your earnings as an expense. The carer must not be your spouse, partner, parent, child or sibling.

Example

You earn £100 a week (after tax, National Insurance and other expenses) and you spend £60 a week on care while you work. You can treat £50 of this as an expense.

You do not count these as earnings:

- money from an occupational or private pension

- help towards your living costs or rent from someone you live with (they cannot be a tenant or boarder)

- the first £20 a week and 50% of the rest of any income you get from someone boarding in your home

- a loan or advance payment from your employer

### If you get State Pension

You cannot get the full amount of both Carer's Allowance and your State Pension at the same time.

- If your pension is £86.45 a week or more, you will not get a Carer's Allowance payment.
- If your pension is less than £86.45 a week, you'll get a Carer's Allowance payment to make up the difference.

### If you get Pension Credit

If your State Pension is more than £86.45 a week, you will not get any Carer's Allowance payments. Your Pension Credit payments will increase instead.

Pension Credit tops up:

- your weekly income to £238 if you're single

- your weekly income for you and your partner together to £363.25 if you have a partner

You may get extra amounts if you have other responsibilities and costs.

The top up and extra amounts are called 'Guarantee Credit'.

### If you have a severe disability

You could get an extra £86.05 a week if you get any of these benefits:

- Attendance Allowance
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA)
- the daily living component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- the daily living component of Adult Disability Payment
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance

## If you care for another adult

You could get an extra £48.15 a week if any of these apply to you:

- you get Carer's Allowance

- you get Carer Support Payment

- you have claimed Carer's Allowance but you do not get paid because another benefit already pays you a higher amount

If you and your partner have both claimed or are getting Carer's Allowance, you can both get this extra amount.

## If you're responsible for children or young people

You can get extra money for each child or young person you're responsible for who lives with you.

You'll get £69.98 a week for each child or young person. For the first child, this goes up to £81.07 a week if they were born before 6 April 2017.

You'll get this extra money until the 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday
- 19th birthday, if they're in eligible education or training – for example, studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

If they're in education, it must be for more than 12 hours a week on average.

### If the child or young person is disabled

You can also get extra money if the child or young person is disabled.

You can get an extra £37.93 a week if they get:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children – lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Child Disability Payment – lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance – lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) – standard rate of the daily living component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Adult Disability Payment – standard rate of the daily living component, or any rate of the mobility component

You can get an extra £118.46 a week if they get:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children – highest rate of the care component
- Child Disability Payment – highest rate of the care component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance – highest rate of the care component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) – enhanced rate of the daily living component
- Adult Disability Payment – enhanced rate of the daily living component

You may also be able to get this if they're blind or severely sight impaired.

## If you have housing costs

You might get extra money to help with your housing costs. This can cover things like:

- ground rent if your property is a leasehold

- some service charges

- charges for tents and site rents

The extra amount you could get depends on your housing costs.

If you get Pension Credit, you might also qualify for:

- Council Tax Reduction

- Housing Benefit if you rent the property you live in

- Support for Mortgage Interest if you own the property you live in

## If you have savings or a second pension

You could get the 'Savings Credit' part of Pension Credit if both of these things are true:

- you reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016

- you saved some money for retirement, for example a personal or workplace pension

If you're single, you'll get up to £17.96 a week in Savings Credit. If you have a partner, you'll get up to £20.10 a week.

You might still get some Savings Credit even if you do not get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit.

## Other help if you get Pension Credit

If you get Pension Credit, you will automatically get cold weather payments.

You can also:

-
apply for a free TV licence if you're aged 75 or over

-
get help with NHS costs if you get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit

NHS costs can include things such as prescriptions, dental treatment, glasses and transport costs for hospital appointments.

## Get help with extra amounts

If you're not sure whether you can get extra amounts, call the Pension Service helpline.

Pension Service helpline

Telephone: 0800 99 1234

If you cannot hear or speak on the phone, use Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 99 1234

If you're on a computer, you can use the British Sign Language (BSL) video relay service. Find out how to use it on a mobile or tablet.

Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm (except public holidays)

Find out about call charges

SMP is paid for up to 39 weeks. You get:

- 90% of your average weekly earnings (before tax) for the first 6 weeks

- £194.32 or 90% of your average weekly earnings — whichever is lower — for the next 33 weeks

SMP is paid the same way as your wages, for example monthly or weekly. Tax and National Insurance will be deducted.

Use the maternity planner to work out how much maternity pay you could get.

If you take Shared Parental Leave, you'll get Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP). ShPP is £194.32 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings — whichever is lower.

### Start date

SMP usually starts when you take your maternity leave.

It also starts automatically if you are off work for a pregnancy-related illness. This can happen in the 4 weeks before the week your baby is due. That week runs from Sunday to Saturday.

## Problems and disputes

You can ask your employer to explain your SMP if you think the amount is wrong.

You can contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team if:

- you disagree about the amount, or
- your employer cannot pay you (for example because they are insolvent).

If you're eligible, you can get either £123.25 a week or 80% of your normal weekly earnings – whichever is lower. This is called Statutory Sick Pay (SSP). It's paid for up to 28 weeks.

You'll be paid SSP for all the full days you're off sick that you normally would have worked.

Your employer will work out how much you get using your average weekly earnings over an 8-week period. You can still get SSP if you started your job recently and have not yet had 8 weeks' pay. Ask your employer to find out more.

### How you get paid

Your employer pays SSP the same way they pay your usual wages. For example, weekly or monthly.

If you have more than one job, you may get SSP from each employer.

Tax and National Insurance will be taken off.

If you think you are not getting the right amount of SSP, talk to your employer. If you are still not happy, contact the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) enquiry line.

The hourly rate for the minimum wage depends on your age and whether you're an apprentice.

This page is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

You must be at least:

- school leaving age to get the National Minimum Wage

- aged 21 to get the National Living Wage

The minimum wage will still apply for workers aged 20 and under.

## Current rates

The rates change every year on 1 April.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2026 | £12.71 | £10.85 | £8 | £8 |
| April 2027 | £13.21 | £11.27 | £8.31 | £8.31 |

### Apprentices

An apprentice gets the apprentice rate if they are either one of these:

- under 19 years old
- 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 is in the first year of their apprenticeship. They get the minimum hourly rate of £8.

An apprentice gets the minimum wage for their age if both of these are true:

- they are aged 19 or over
- they have completed the first year of their apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 has completed the first year of their apprenticeship. They get the minimum hourly rate of £12.71.

## Previous rates

These are the rates for the National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage from April 2019.

### Rates between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2026

Since 1 April 2024, the National Living Wage applies to people aged 21 and over.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |

| April 2025 to March 2026 | £12.21 | £10 | £7.55 | £7.55 |

| April 2024 to March 2025 | £11.44 | £8.60 | £6.40 | £6.40 |

### Rates between 1 April 2021 and 31 March 2024

Between 1 April 2021 and 31 March 2024, the National Living Wage applied to people aged 23 and over.

| | 23 and over | 21 to 22 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |

| April 2023 to March 2024 | £10.42 | £10.18 | £7.49 | £5.28 | £5.28 |

| April 2022 to March 2023 | £9.50 | £9.18 | £6.83 | £4.81 | £4.81 |

| April 2021 to March 2022 | £8.91 | £8.36 | £6.56 | £4.62 | £4.30 |

### Rates before 1 April 2021

Before 1 April 2021, the National Living Wage applied to people aged 25 and over.

| | 25 and over | 21 to 24 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |

| April 2020 to March 2021 | £8.72 | £8.20 | £6.45 | £4.55 | £4.15 |

| April 2019 to March 2020 | £8.21 | £7.70 | £6.15 | £4.35 | £3.90 |

## Who gets the minimum wage

Read this to find out who is entitled to the minimum wage.

You can use the minimum wage calculator to check if the National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage is being paid.

Contact Acas if you're not getting the National Minimum Wage and think you should be.

You will get a letter telling you how much Winter Fuel Payment you will get. The letter comes in October or November. You only get this letter if you are eligible for the payment.

If you do not get the letter but think you should, check if you need to make a claim.

How much money you get depends on two things:

- when you were born
- your circumstances between 21 to 27 September 2026

This period is called the 'qualifying week'.

Marriage Allowance lets you give £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner. Your Personal Allowance is the amount you can earn before paying tax.

This cuts their tax by up to £252 in the tax year (6 April to 5 April the next year).

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

To benefit as a couple, you (as the lower earner) must normally have an income below your Personal Allowance. The Personal Allowance is usually £12,570.

You can work out how much tax you could save as a couple. You should call the Income Tax helpline instead if you get other income, like dividends, savings or benefits from your job. You can also call if you do not know what your taxable income is.

When you give some of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner, you might have to pay more tax yourself. But you could still pay less tax as a couple.

**Example**

Your income is £11,500 and your Personal Allowance is £12,570, so you do not pay tax.

Your partner's income is £20,000 and their Personal Allowance is £12,570, so they pay tax on £7,430 (their 'taxable income'). This means as a couple you are paying Income Tax on £7,430.

When you claim Marriage Allowance, you give £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your partner. Your Personal Allowance becomes £11,310 and your partner gets a reduction of £1,260 on their taxable income.

This means you will now pay tax on £190, but your partner will only pay tax on £6,170. As a couple you benefit, as you only pay Income Tax on £6,360 rather than £7,430. This saves you £214 in tax.

## Who can apply

You can benefit from Marriage Allowance if all of the following apply:

- you're married or in a civil partnership

- you do not pay Income Tax, or your income is below your Personal Allowance (usually £12,570)

- your partner pays Income Tax at the basic rate, which usually means their income is between £12,571 and £50,270 before they receive Marriage Allowance

You cannot claim Marriage Allowance if you live together but you are not married and not in a civil partnership.

If you live in Scotland, your partner must pay the starter, basic or intermediate rate. This usually means their income is between £12,571 and £43,662.

It will not affect your application for Marriage Allowance if you or your partner:

- are currently receiving a pension

- live abroad — as long as you get a Personal Allowance

If you or your partner were born before 6 April 1935, you might benefit more as a couple by applying for Married Couple's Allowance instead.

You cannot get Marriage Allowance and Married Couple's Allowance at the same time.

### Backdating your claim

You can start your claim for any year from 6 April 2022 (the 2022 to 2023 tax year) where you were eligible for Marriage Allowance.

Your partner's tax bill will go down, based on the Personal Allowance rate for each year you go back to.

If your partner has died since 5 April 2022, you can still claim — phone the Income Tax helpline. If your partner was the lower earner, the person in charge of their tax affairs must phone.

### Stopping Marriage Allowance

Your Personal Allowance will transfer to your partner automatically every year. This will happen until you cancel Marriage Allowance.

You might cancel it if:

- your income changes, or
- your relationship ends.

## If you pay basic rate Income Tax

If you're a basic rate taxpayer, the rate you pay on gains from 6 April 2026 depends on how big your gain is and how much taxable income you have.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

To work out your rate:

- Find your taxable income. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any other Income Tax reliefs you're entitled to.

- Find your total taxable gains.

- Take away your tax-free allowance from your total taxable gains.

- Add the amount left to your taxable income.

- If this amount is within the basic Income Tax band, you'll pay 18% on your gains made from 6 April 2026.

- For any amount above the basic Income Tax band, you'll pay 24% on gains made from 6 April 2026.

### Example 1

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income is £20,000. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs. Your taxable gains are £12,600.

First, take the Capital Gains tax-free allowance away from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000. This leaves £9,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The combined amount is £29,600. This is less than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year). So you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18%.

This means you'll pay £1,728 in Capital Gains Tax.

### Example 2

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income is £20,000. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs. Your taxable gains are £52,600.

First, take the Capital Gains tax-free allowance away from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000. This leaves £49,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The combined amount is £69,600. This is more than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year). So you will pay Capital Gains Tax at 18% on £17,700 and then 24% on £31,900.

This means you will pay £10,842.

Inheritance Tax is a tax on the estate of someone who has died. The estate is everything they owned — their property, money and possessions.

You normally pay no Inheritance Tax if either:

- the value of the estate is below the £325,000 threshold
- you leave everything above the £325,000 threshold to your spouse, civil partner, a charity or a community amateur sports club

You may still need to report the estate's value even if it's below the threshold.

If you give away your home to your children (including adopted, foster or stepchildren) or grandchildren your threshold can increase to £500,000.

If you're married or in a civil partnership and your estate is worth less than your threshold, any unused threshold can be added to your partner's threshold when you die.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## Inheritance Tax rates

The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%. It is only charged on the part of your estate that is above the threshold.

### Example

Your estate is worth £500,000 and your tax-free threshold is £325,000. The Inheritance Tax charged will be 40% of £175,000 (£500,000 minus £325,000).

Some assets in your estate can pay a lower rate of Inheritance Tax — 36% — if you leave 10% or more of the net value to charity in your will. The net value is the total value of your estate minus any debts you owe.

### Reliefs and exemptions

Some gifts you give while you are alive may be taxed after your death. Depending on when you gave the gift, taper relief may mean the Inheritance Tax on that gift is less than 40%.

Other reliefs, such Business Relief or Agricultural Relief, mean some assets can be passed on with no Inheritance Tax, or with a lower amount to pay.

## Who pays the tax to HMRC

The tax is paid to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) using money from your estate. The person who deals with your estate pays it. If there's a will, this person is called the 'executor'.

Your beneficiaries (the people who inherit your estate) do not normally pay tax on the things they inherit. They may have related taxes to pay. For example, if they get rental income from a house left to them in a will.

People you give gifts to might have to pay Inheritance Tax, but only if you give away more than £325,000 and die within 7 years.

### What's Extra Help?

Extra Help is a Medicare program. It helps people with limited income and resources pay for Part D costs. Part D is Medicare drug coverage. Extra Help can pay for premiums, deductibles, coinsurance, and other costs.

If you get Extra Help, you also won't have to pay Part D late enrollment penalties.

Some people get Extra Help automatically. Other people must apply for it.

Extra Help isn't available in Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, or American Samoa. But other programs in those areas can help people with limited income and resources. The programs are different in each area. Call your State Medical Assistance (Medicaid) office to learn more.

- Full-benefit Medicaid coverage
- Help from your state paying your Part B premiums (from a Medicare Savings Program)
- Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments from Social Security

You'll get a notice in the mail about your Extra Help. It tells you how much you'll pay. It also tells you your new Medicare drug plan, if you don't have one already.

If you don't get Extra Help automatically, you can apply for it:

Apply for Extra Help

You can also contact your local State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) to get free help applying.

You can apply for Extra Help and Medicare Savings Programs (MSPs) at the same time. These state programs help with other Medicare costs.

When you apply for Extra Help, Social Security will send information to your state to start an MSP application unless you tell them not to on the Extra Help application. Learn more about Medicare Savings Programs.

You should sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period. You do not have to if you have other coverage that is similar in value to Medicare, like from an employer. If you do not sign up and you do not have that other coverage, you may have to pay a late enrollment penalty.

Late enrollment penalties:

- Are added to your monthly premium.
- Are not a one-time late fee.
- Are usually charged for as long as you have that type of coverage. For most people, that means you pay it for life. The Part A penalty is different.
- Go up the longer you wait to sign up. They are based on how long you go without coverage similar to Medicare. Find out when you should sign up to avoid penalties.

## Part A late enrollment penalty

- Some people have to buy Part A because they don't get it for free.
- If you have to buy Part A, and you don't buy it when you're first eligible for Medicare, your monthly premium may go up 10%.
- You'll have to pay the penalty for twice the number of years you didn't sign up.

**Example:**

If you were eligible for Part A for 2 years but didn't sign up, you'll have to pay the higher premium for 4 years.

You usually don't have to pay a penalty if you meet certain conditions that let you sign up for Part A during a Special Enrollment Period. Find out if you're eligible for a Special Enrollment Period.

## Part B late enrollment penalty

- You won't have to pay a Part B penalty if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, or if you enroll in a Medicare Savings Program. Learn more about Special Enrollment Periods.
- You'll pay an extra 10% for each year you could have signed up for Part B but didn't.
- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.

Example:

If you waited 2 full years (24 months) to sign up for Part B and didn't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you'll have to pay a 20% late enrollment penalty. That's 10% for each full 12-month period you could have signed up. You'll also pay the standard Part B monthly premium ($202.90 in 2026).

2026 Calculation:

$202.90 (2026 Part B standard premium)
+ $40.58 (20% late enrollment penalty, which is 20% of $202.90)

$243.48

$243.50 will be your Part B monthly premium for 2026. This amount ($243.48) is rounded to the nearest $.10 and includes the late enrollment penalty.

## Part D late enrollment penalty

- Generally, you won't have to pay a Part D penalty if:

  - You have creditable drug coverage (coverage that's similar in value to Part D) OR
  - You qualify for Extra Help

- You'll pay an extra 1% for each month (that's 12% a year) if you:

  - Don't join a Medicare drug plan when you first get Medicare.
  - Go 63 days or more without creditable drug coverage.

- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.
- After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you have to pay a penalty and what your premium will be.

What if I don't agree with the Part D late enrollment penalty?

Example:
If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a Medicare drug plan, and you didn't have creditable drug coverage, you'll have to pay a 14% late enrollment penalty in addition to your monthly plan premium.

- The penalty amount comes from the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026).
- The national base beneficiary premium changes each year, so your penalty amount may also change each year. This monthly penalty is added for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage, even if you switch plans.

In 2026:

$38.99 (2026 national base beneficiary premium)
X   0.14 (14% penalty)

$5.46 (rounded to the nearest $0.10 = $5.50)
$5.50 will be your monthly penalty for 2026. This amount is added to your plan's monthly premium for 2026.

## Am I eligible?

To join a Medicare health plan or drug plan, you generally must:

- Have Medicare Part A and/or Part B.

- Be a U.S. citizen or U.S. national, a lawful permanent resident (green card holder), a Cuban-Haitian entrant, or lawfully living in the U.S. as a Compact of Free Association (COFA) migrant.

- Live in the service area of the plan you want to join.

- Have your Medicare Number and your Part A and/or Part B coverage start dates. You can find this information on your Medicare card.

### When can I join?

You can only join, switch, or drop a health or drug plan if it is one of these:

- A Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C), with or without drug coverage
- Another Medicare health plan
- A Medicare drug plan

You can only do this at certain times. These times are called enrollment periods.

## Initial Enrollment Period

This is usually when you turn 65.

It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65. You may be able to get Medicare earlier if you have a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), or ALS (also called Lou Gehrig's disease). Learn more about when you can sign up in these situations.

You can join any plan, but you need:

- Both Part A and Part B to join a Medicare Advantage Plan, with or without drug coverage.
- Either Part A or Part B to join a Medicare drug plan.

When your coverage starts:

- If you ask to join a plan before your Part A and/or Part B starts: Your plan coverage starts the same day your Part A and/or Part B starts.
- If you ask to join a plan after your Part A and/or Part B starts: Your plan coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets your request.

## Initial Enrollment Period – New to Part B

This is for you if you already have Part A and want to add Part B later.

Your enrollment period starts 3 months before the month you first become eligible for both Part A and Part B. You have 2 months after you get both Part A and Part B for the first time to join a plan.

You can:

Join any Medicare Advantage Plan, with or without drug coverage.

Coverage starts:

Generally, it starts on the first of the month after the plan gets your request to join.

If you joined a Medicare Advantage Plan during your Initial Enrollment Period, you can change to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) or go back to Original Medicare (with or without a drug plan) within the first 3 months you have Medicare Part A and Part B.

###  What do I need to know about drug coverage?

You have creditable prescription drug coverage. As long as you keep it, you can wait to join a Medicare drug plan or a Medicare Advantage Plan with drug coverage.

- If you are not sure your current drug plan is creditable, ask your plan. They have to tell you. They will also send you this information every year.
- Keep the information your current drug plan sends you. You may need it when you are ready to join a Medicare drug plan. Do not send this information to Medicare.

You won't pay the Part D late enrollment penalty as long as you don't go more than 63 days without creditable drug coverage. Learn how to avoid the late enrollment penalty.

## Your first chance to sign up (Initial Enrollment Period)

You can sign up when you turn 65. This is called your Initial Enrollment Period. It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.

Avoid the penalty
If you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, you may have to wait to sign up and you may have to pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage. The penalty goes up the longer you wait. You may also have to pay a penalty if you have to pay a Part A premium, which is also called "Premium-Part A."  Learn more about how to avoid late enrollment penalties. 

### When your coverage starts

The month you sign up during your Initial Enrollment Period determines when your coverage starts. Coverage always starts on the first of the month.

If you qualify for premium-free Part A: Your Part A coverage starts the month you turn 65. If your birthday is on the first of the month, coverage starts the month before you turn 65.

Part B (and premium-Part A): Coverage starts based on the month you sign up:

| If you sign up: | Coverage starts: |
| Before the month you turn 65 | The month you turn 65 |
| The month you turn 65, or during the 3 months after | The next month |

### Signing up for premium-free Part A later

You can sign up for Part A any time after you turn 65. Your Part A coverage starts 6 months back from when you sign up or when you apply for benefits from Social Security (or the Railroad Retirement Board). Coverage can't start earlier than the month you turned 65.

## Between January 1-March 31 each year (General Enrollment Period)

You can sign up for Medicare between January 1-March 31 each year. This time is called the General Enrollment Period. Your coverage starts the month after you sign up. You might pay a monthly late enrollment penalty if you don't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.

## Joining a plan

After you sign up for Medicare, you can join a health or drug plan, but only at certain times.

- To join a Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C), you need both Part A and Part B.
- To join a Medicare drug plan (Part D), you only need Part A or Part B.

Find out when you can join a plan.

Your total costs for Medicare drug coverage depend on which plan you pick. Depending on the plan, you could pay:

- Premium: A monthly amount you pay for coverage. You pay this whether you get covered drugs or not.

- Your specific premium depends on the plan you pick. You may have to pay more depending on your income. Who pays a higher Part D premium because of income?
- If you have to pay a Part D late enrollment penalty, it will be added to your monthly premium.

Tip: Even if you don't take many drugs now, or your current out-of-pocket drug costs are low, consider getting a drug plan with a low monthly premium. This can help you avoid the late enrollment penalty. All plans must cover a wide range of drugs that people with Medicare take.

- Deductible: An amount you pay for covered drugs and items each year before your plan starts to pay. Your deductible depends on which plan you pick. No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $700 in 2027 ($615 in 2026), and some plans have no deductible.
- Copayment: A fixed amount you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.
- Coinsurance: A percentage you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.

## Medicare drug coverage stages

Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage Plans with drug coverage usually have 3 stages:

- Deductible stage: If your Medicare plan has a deductible, you pay all out-of-pocket costs until you reach the full deductible. No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $615 in 2026 ($700 in 2027). Some Medicare drug plans don't have a deductible.
- Initial coverage stage: After you reach your full deductible (if your plan has a deductible), you'll pay 25% of the cost as coinsurance for your generic and brand-name drugs. This continues until your out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs reaches $2,100 in 2026 ($2,400 in 2027). This amount includes certain payments made on your behalf, like through the Extra Help program. Then, you'll automatically get "catastrophic coverage."
- Catastrophic coverage stage: You won't have to pay out-of-pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

When you have Medicare drug coverage, you'll get an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) the month after the pharmacy bills your plan. Your EOB shows:

- the prescriptions you filled
- what your plan paid
- what you and others have paid
- your coverage stage
- what counts toward your out-of-pocket costs and your total drug costs

## How do I pay your plan's premium?

You can choose to pay your premium by:

- Having your plan take it from your checking or savings account.
- Charging it to a credit or debit card. Fees may apply.
- Getting a bill each month from your plan. Some plans bill you for next month's coverage before it starts. Send your payment to the plan. Do not send it to Medicare. Contact your plan to get their payment address.
- Having your plan take your premium out of your Social Security payment. Contact your plan to ask for this. Do not contact Social Security. It may take up to 3 months to start. In cases where your premiums weren't withheld from your Social Security payment until 1 or 2 months after you joined a Medicare drug plan, you will get a bill for those months. You need to pay your drug plan's monthly premium directly to your plan for those months. Your plan will tell you when your premium withholding from your Social Security payment is set up.

## How can I lower my drug costs?

If you qualify, there are programs that can lower your drug costs:

- **Medicaid:** A joint federal and state program. It helps cover medical costs for some people with limited income and resources. Each state has different income and resource requirements. These set who's eligible. Contact your state to find out if you qualify.

- **Extra Help:** A Medicare program. It helps pay your drug costs. You automatically qualify for Extra Help if you qualify for Medicaid, one of the Medicare Savings Programs, or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits from Social Security. If you don't automatically qualify, you can apply.

- **Medicare's Limited Income Newly Eligible Transition (LI NET):** A Medicare program. It gives temporary Medicare Part D drug coverage. This is for people who qualify for Extra Help or Medicaid but aren't enrolled in a Medicare drug plan yet. LI NET covers all Part D covered drugs. There are no network pharmacy restrictions.

- **State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (SPAP):** These programs give coverage from your state (or the U.S. Virgin Islands). They help pay your drug plan premiums and/or cost sharing. SPAP contributions may count toward your Medicare drug coverage out-of-pocket limit. Eligibility depends on each program's specific rules.

- **Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (sometimes called Patient Assistance Programs (PAPs)):** Some pharmaceutical companies offer programs. These help pay for medications for people enrolled in Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Find out if there's a PAP that can lower prescription costs for the drugs you take. Each company has different eligibility requirements. Contact the company to find out if you're eligible and start getting help.

The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan is a new payment option. It works with your current Medicare drug coverage. It helps you manage your out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by your plan by spreading them across the calendar year (January–December). This payment option might help you manage your monthly expenses, but it doesn't save you money or lower your drug costs.

## What's the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The Part D late enrollment penalty is money that gets permanently added to your Medicare drug coverage (Part D) premium.

You may owe a late enrollment penalty if, at any time after your Initial Enrollment Period is over, there is a period of 63 or more days in a row when you don't have Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage.

After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you have to pay a penalty and what your premium will be.

You'll generally have to pay the penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.

### How much is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The penalty is calculated like this:

- 1% × the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026) × the number of full, uncovered months you were eligible to join Medicare drug coverage but didn't (and didn't have other creditable prescription drug coverage).

That amount is rounded to the nearest $.10 and added to your monthly premium.

The "national base beneficiary premium" may go up each year, so your penalty amount may go up each year too.

## Appeal when a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient with observation services"

A court order gives you the right to appeal if a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient" and you also meet certain criteria.

You can ask for an appeal if you were admitted to the hospital as an inpatient on or after January 1, 2009, and the hospital changed your status to "outpatient getting observation services" (and you meet certain other criteria). Learn how to file this type of appeal.

You can ask for a fast appeal if you are still in the hospital. This applies if you were admitted to the hospital as an inpatient and the hospital changed your status to "outpatient getting observation services." Learn how to file this type of appeal.

### Why does hospital status matter?

Your hospital status helps decide how much you pay for hospital care. Your hospital status may also affect whether Medicare will cover care you get in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) after your hospital stay.
